title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap, provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑based success rates. The run used deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), recorded in the archived execution artifacts. No preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and therefore no guarded exclusions or replacements were applied. All 150 baseline and matched guarded episodes passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Critically, because the executed sampling provenance and shared‑generation semantics are documented in the archive, we explicitly reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test (H2) as uninformative/degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination in this execution; the observed null therefore reflects execution choices rather than evidence that public benchmarks are contamination‑free. We report artifact‑anchored diagnostics and recommend concrete, implementable design changes to make future audits sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps problems such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Reliable deployment decisions require that benchmarked performance reflect model capability rather than dataset contamination (templated leakage or memorized items). Surveys and recent benchmark studies highlight contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommend deterministic detectors, provenance tracing, and validator oracles.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored confirmatory audit asking: under conservative, preregistered deterministic detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap with prespecified thresholds; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy (exclude only high‑confidence flags), how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item sample and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? Our contributions are (1) a fully preregistered experiment (study_id = contamination‑audit‑netops‑2026‑v1) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 using a deterministic NetOps validator; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that documents why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes artifact‑grounded design changes to increase audit sensitivity.

Scope and bounded claims. The preregistered plan permitted sampling from public NetOps benchmarks (four OpenAlex items listed in benchmark_scope). The executed run instead used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (each task carries source_identifier "synthetic-netops:"), and used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false). These execution facts are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json (see archived bundle). Because of these documented choices, the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome applies only to the executed synthetic + shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM→NetOps translation and repair. Prior work shows that LLMs can produce configuration artifacts from high‑level intent and can propose repairs; integrating formal verification or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality versus naive generation [https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W7157506260]. Formal network verification tools (Header Space Analysis, localized subspecification) are practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly used in generate–validate pipelines [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659, https://openalex.org/W2742515467].

Evaluation validity and contamination. Recent surveys and conceptual frameworks emphasize contamination and construct‑validity risks for LLM benchmarks (hallucination, templating, and overlap with pretraining corpora) and recommend deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance checks, and conservative reporting [https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Our study implements a conservative subset of these defenses within a preregistered generate→detect→guard pipeline and focuses on an artifact‑anchored reconciliation when execution choices render the primary test uninformative.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The experiment was preregistered (study_id = contamination‑audit‑netops‑2026‑v1). The primary estimand was the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs and the prespecified confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) was also preregistered. Planned confirmatory accounting: task_count = 150, planned_episode_count = 300 (baseline + guarded), maximum_model_calls = 300.

Sampling and executed deviation. The preregistration allowed deterministic or public sampling. The preregistered benchmark_scope listed four public OpenAlex datasets (see preregistration evidence_record_ids). The executed run, however, sampled 150 deterministic synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry carries source_identifier with prefix "synthetic-netops:". This choice is documented in execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The execution therefore deviated from the scenario of sampling web‑sourced public items: that deviation is recorded in the archive (execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json) and is reported here as an explicit preregistration→execution disclosure rather than as an unrecorded change. No formal amendment artifact is present in the bundle authorizing a switch to public datasets; the sampling change is reflected by the generated task records in the archive.

Generation semantics and practical consequences. The preregistration allowed either independent_condition_generation (separate generation per condition) or shared generation semantics. The executed model_configuration.json sets independent_condition_generation = false, i.e., shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under those semantics the pipeline performs a single model generation per item and reuses that candidate for both baseline and guarded episodes unless an exclusion/replacement is triggered. This reduced model_calls_used to 150 (one shared call per item) from the preregistered maximum of 300 and mechanically collapses baseline vs guarded discordance when no high‑confidence flags occur; execution accounting is recorded (execution/manifest fields: planned_episode_count = 300, completed_episode_count = 300, model_calls_used = 150).

Contamination detectors and persistence policy. The preregistered detector suite comprised: (1) exact normalized token equality (canonicalize whitespace/tokens); (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and lower thresholds for sensitivity analyses; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps/DOIs to model public cutoff heuristics. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when thresholds were crossed or a replacement was invoked (detector persistence behavior is recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json). Consequently, when the execution produced no high‑confidence flags, no global per‑item overlap table was written to the archive; the absence of such a table is an artifact of the detector persistence policy and is documented in the transformation manifest.

Guarded exclusion and replacement. The preregistration required deterministic exclusion only for high‑confidence flags (exact match OR 5‑gram ≥ 0.80) with deterministic retemplating replacements sampled via fixed seeds; replacements needed to pass an embedding similarity (cosine ≥ 0.85) before acceptance. Because no high‑confidence flags occurred in this run, no replacements were performed (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty), a fact recorded in the archived artifacts.

Validator and scoring rule. The deterministic oracle used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). For each candidate configuration the validator parsed commands, simulated state updates on an explicit device model, checked required_final_state fields and workflow constraints, and emitted a binary pass/fail plus detailed traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, normalized_configuration). The scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation required matching expected_final_state on allowed fields and respecting workflow/transient constraints; these trace fields underpin the binary outcomes archived under execution/scoring/*.json.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item) rather than two independent generations per item; provider and reconciliation artifacts confirm these counts (execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Contamination detector outputs. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags for the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows. Because the detector workflow persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlaps only on threshold crossings, the archive does not contain a full per‑item overlap distribution for this run — this missingness is explained by the detector persistence policy recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json and is not an unexplained omission.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency table: n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode responses and validator traces supporting these numbers are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/scoring/*.json).

Reclassification of the primary test. Because the executed sampling provenance (synthetic tasks) and shared_initial_candidate semantics are artifact‑recorded, the prespecified primary confirmatory test (H2) is uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in this execution: when baseline and guarded conditions reuse an identical generation per item, no discordant pairs can arise absent exclusions. We therefore reclassify H2 as degenerate/untestable for the executed run and frame the reported McNemar statistics as an artifact‑diagnostic outcome rather than as substantive evidence about contamination in web‑sourced public benchmarks.
sections.discussion:
Mechanism of degeneracy and diagnostic implications. Two documented execution choices produced the observed concordance (n11 = 150): (1) provenance‑stable synthetic sampling (each task source_identifier = "synthetic-netops:") and (2) shared_initial_candidate generation (independent_condition_generation = false). Both facts are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json. Under these conditions the guarded exclusion policy could not produce discordant outputs because no independent generation per condition occurred and no high‑confidence flags were triggered. The artifact record therefore explains the degenerate null without invoking model general claims.

Why the per‑item overlap table is absent. The detector implementation persisted full per‑item fuzzy overlap scores only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred; this persistence policy, documented in execution/transformation_manifest.json, means a global per‑item overlap table is not present in the archive for this run. The practical consequence is that readers cannot retroactively inspect how close items were to the high‑confidence threshold; this deficiency motivates a simple workflow change: persist all per‑item overlap scores irrespective of threshold crossings so future audits can report overlap distributions and sensitivity curves.

Design changes to restore audit sensitivity (artifact‑anchored recommendations). The archived artifacts support the following implementable changes: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs with timestamps) instead of or in addition to synthetic items so provenance heuristics can meaningfully discriminate pretraining‑era evidence; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true to ensure baseline and guarded outputs are independently realized and therefore enable observation of generation‑level discordance; (c) persist all per‑item fuzzy overlap scores in analysis/contamination_scores.csv regardless of threshold crossings; (d) expand to multi‑model replication and multiple generation seeds to increase independent trial counts and power; and (e) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from explicit gaps visible in the archived execution (model_calls_used = 150, empty contamination_summary.csv, absence of global overlap table).

Operational implication and caution. The run confirms that a deterministic validator can record detailed traces confirming functional correctness for generated configurations; however, passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 does not imply production readiness beyond the validator's enforced properties. More generally, auditors must avoid extrapolating synthetic+shared‑generation nulls to public benchmarks: our artifact‑anchored diagnosis shows that audit sensitivity depends on sampling provenance and generation semantics.

Reproducibility and artifact guidance. All code, seeds, model_configuration.json, task_manifest.jsonl, raw responses, scoring traces, analysis artifacts, and reconciliation logs are archived in the execution bundle (see execution_manifest entries). The detector persistence behavior is recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json, and the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Future auditors can rerun the same pipeline with independent_condition_generation = true and public sampling to obtain non‑degenerate paired comparisons when contamination exists.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline; 150/150 guarded). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics (both recorded in the archive) and therefore does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. We explicitly reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as uninformative/degenerate for this execution. We provide an artifact‑grounded reconciliation, confirm deterministic reconciliation checks passed, and recommend concrete design changes—provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, multi‑model replication, full per‑item overlap persistence, and paraphrase‑sensitive detectors—to increase audit sensitivity in future preregistered runs. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement below.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed under the autonomous preregistration contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the archived bundle). Declared LLM: gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (version 5.0). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0). Key archived artifacts referenced in the manuscript include execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/contamination_summary.csv; the full execution bundle contains raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and the transformation manifest. Exact immutable initial master‑prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) were selected by the human Research Director prior to the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, replacement rules, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline and are included in the execution bundle. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or this Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred (permitted) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence for this final study unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The execution followed preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; the archive records no deviations other than the documented sampling and generation semantics used in execution.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance, paraphrase‑robust detectors, or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
